catalog_quote: Part of the language’s morphemes feature stress as one of their permanent phonological properties. Morphemes that feature stress are almost always stressed (but see below for cases of stressed morphemes that may be left unstressed in discourse), while morphemes that do not feature stress never are. Whether a morpheme belongs to the category of stressed morphemes or unstressed morphemes is not a lexical property, but rather depends on the nature of that morpheme; this distribution is explained below. The position of stress within a stressed morpheme is determined automatically and is absolutely fixed. Stressed morphemes always bear stress on their first syllable. Consequently, stress position cannot create contrasts between morphemes. sweep_summary: Ticuna (ticu1245) is not in the catalog. Of the four title-works with stress in the title: (1) Rodrigues & Martins 1999 'vogais acentuadas de Braga' is a European Portuguese (Braga) acoustic study, mis-assigned to Ticuna by Glottolog's own 'computerized assignment from acustico' -- irrelevant, priority none. (2) Soares 1996 (Letras de Hoje 31(2): 7-26; real title 'Regulação rítmica e ATUAÇÃO do OCP em Tikuna') was found open on the PUCRS OJS site, downloaded (scan, no text layer; scanned with tesseract at 300 dpi and checked against the page image) and. p. 21 states that a rule makes the leftmost syllable of a root the stress bearer, stress being interpreted as long duration. (3) Soares 2000 (Editora da UNICAMP book, Vol. I = syntax) not located online; print only, low priority because it is the book edition of (4). (4) Soares 1992 UNICAMP thesis was already held by the project (etnolinguistica.org scan with text layer; official copy also at DOI 10.47749/t/unicamp.1992.46445) and read: Vol. II p. 607 'A sílaba mais à esquerda de uma raiz é portadora de acento', with the consequence (p. 616) that stress is usually penultimate since roots are mostly disyllabic, antepenultimate in monosyllable+disyllable compounds, and monosyllabic content words are stressed/long. Best first-hand statement read: Skilton 2023 PDA §4 p. 15 (fixed initial stress on the Prosodic Word = root-initial for most classes, duration the primary correlate, with measurements), converging with Soares 1992/1996 and Bertet 2020 pp. 83-85 (stressed morphemes always stressed on their first syllable; demarcative). searches were done by automated download/direct download against the journal archive, Glottolog, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Open Library.

new_statements.quote: The position of stress within a stressed morpheme is determined automatically and is absolutely fixed. Stressed morphemes always bear stress on their first syllable. Consequently, stress position cannot create contrasts between morphemes. The first syllable of independent morphemes—i.e. morphemes that may be uttered on their own, including in particular verbs and independent nouns—is regularly stressed, as in examples (33a–33f). The main phonological function of stress is therefore not a contrastive one, but a demarcative one: stress signals the beginning of independent morphemes.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ticuna is a tone language (10 tonemes in stressed syllables, 6 in unstressed per Bertet; 5 level tones per Skilton) that also has non-contrastive, demarcative word stress fixed on the first syllable of the lexical root / independent morpheme (= first syllable of the prosodic word); proclitics precede it unstressed, suffixes/enclitics/bound nouns follow it unstressed; one stress per prosodic word; main correlate is vowel duration. Skilton 2023 (Cushillococha, Peru: 'stress always falls on the first syllable of the PrWd', p.19) and Soares 1992/2020 (Brazil: 'localizado na sílaba mais à esquerda de uma raiz') state the same rule independently.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Bertet: none described (a prosodic word has exactly one stressed syllable). Skilton 2023: no evidence for iterative footing beyond the initial foot. Soares 1992/2020: posits an additional 'acento rítmico' (rhythmic stress, realized as a second long duration) that can appear on suffix strings away from the root stress, built right-to-left in binary feet.
new_statements.exceptions: Bertet: a few dependent morphemes (personal roots, deictic roots, first part of the bipartite deictic verb) are regularly stressed; a few independent function words ('my', 'and', prf) are usually left unstressed in discourse, in which case stress is dropped, never shifted; pre-pausal stressed short vowels are not lengthened. Skilton: inalienable nouns (second member of compounds) never stressed; loanwords may show stress-licensed segments in non-initial syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word = one independent (root) morpheme plus any clitics/affixes; stress is root-initial, hence not necessarily initial in the orthographic/cliticized word (subject proclitics precede the stress). Statements based on both elicited citation forms and spontaneous texts; Skilton adds duration measurements.
new_statements.identity_note: Three first-hand descriptions of three national varieties agree: Bertet 2020 describes the San Martín de Amacayacu variety (Colombia, 'smat'); Skilton 2023 the Cushillococha variety (Peru); Soares 1992/2020 Brazilian Tikuna (upper Solimões). Glottolog treats Ticuna as a single language ticu1245 with no dialect glottocodes; all three describe the same root-/prosodic-word-initial stress in a language with a large tone inventory (5 level tones per Skilton/Anderson; 10 tonemes in stressed syllables per Bertet).

new_statements.quote: Stress in Cushillococha Ticuna is fixed on the initial syllable of the Prosodic Word, which is – for most word classes – the initial syllable of the root (§4.1-4.6). The primary acoustic correlate of stress is duration (§4.7). Phonological consequences of stress are far-reaching, affecting contrast licensing (§5), lexical phonology (§§6-7), and grammatical tone (§8). Other research on varieties of Ticuna describes different stress-tone interactions. For the Cushillococha variety, L. Anderson (1959) and D. Anderson (1962) do not recognize the existence of stress.
new_statements.citation: Skilton, Amalia. 2023. Tone, stress, and their interactions in Cushillococha Ticuna. Phonological Data and Analysis 5(5): 1-44. doi:10.3765/pda.v5art5.58 (CC BY). [Not a title-works with stress in the title; already held by the project from the earlier reading and read in this search of works with stress in the title. Converges with Soares 1992 p. 607 / 1996 p. 21 and Bertet 2020 pp. 83-85, which are this search of works with stress in the title's own statements.]
new_statements.reading: Fixed root/prosodic-word-initial stress (proclitics never stressed; in compounds/inalienable possession only the first stem is stressed), cued primarily by vowel duration (stressed ~159-201 ms vs unstressed ~123 ms), in a language with five (Skilton) to ten/sixteen (Bertet) tonemes. Three independent first-hand descriptions agree: Soares 1992/1996 (Brazilian varieties: leftmost syllable of the root bears stress, realised as length; hence usually penultimate because roots are mostly disyllabic, antepenultimate in monosyllable+disyllable compounds), Bertet 2020 pp. 83-85 (San Martín de Amacayacu, Colombia: stressed morphemes always bear stress on their first syllable; demarcative; duration the main correlate), and Skilton 2023 (Cushillococha, Peru). A catalog entry would be: fixed initial (root-initial) stress, non-contrastive, duration-cued, coexisting with lexical tone; the older SIL descriptions (Anderson 1959/1962) and the Stanford Phonology Archive report no stress information.

sources.note: §2.2 Stress, pp. 83-85: stress is a fixed property of independent morphemes (verbs, independent nouns etc.), always on their first syllable; demarcative not contrastive; one stress per prosodic word; clitics/bound nouns unstressed; correlates = duration (>=1.5x) and to a lesser extent intensity; stressed syllables license 10 tonemes vs 6 in unstressed (§2.4); stress never shifts but a few function words may drop it (§2.5, p.121).

sources.quote: 1. A sílaba mais à esquerda de uma raiz é portadora de acento. 2. Os parâmetros da linha 0 são [+ cabeça terminal, + limitado], dominância à esquerda, construção do constituinte da direita para a esquerda; (esses parâmetros se aplicam utilizando-se a duração e/ou a altura). [...] A primeira regra, por exemplo, faz de uma sílaba mais à esquerda da raiz uma sílaba acentuada. Como a grande maioria das raízes em Tikuna é de dissílabos, a sílaba mais à esquerda da raiz acaba sendo a penúltima. [Translation: 1. The leftmost syllable of a root bears stress. 2. Line-0 parameters are [+terminal head, +bounded], left dominance, constituent construction right-to-left (applied using duration and/or pitch). ... The first rule makes the leftmost syllable of the root a stressed syllable. Since the great majority of Tikuna roots are disyllabic, the leftmost syllable of the root ends up being the penult.] (pp. 607, 616)
sources.locator: Vol. II, p. 607 (PDF p. 872); also p. 526 (PDF 791) and pp. 615-617 (PDF 880-882)
sources.note: Vol. II p.607 (PDF 872): rule '1. A sílaba mais à esquerda de uma raiz é portadora de acento'; pp.615-616 (PDF 880-881): stress realized as long duration on leftmost root syllable; since most roots are disyllabic it usually ends up penultimate, antepenultimate in compounds; content monosyllables long/stressed; metrical constituents built right-to-left below that.

sources.quote: Duração: De acordo com Soares (1992a), a duração longa do núcleo silábico constituído por segmento vocálico deve ser derivada por regra. Em (24), há exemplos de duração longa obtida mediante uma regra que faz da sílaba mais à esquerda de uma raiz a portadora do acento, sendo o acento interpretado como duração longa. [Translation: Duration: According to Soares (1992a), the long duration of a syllable nucleus consisting of a vowel segment must be derived by rule. In (24) there are examples of long duration obtained by a rule that makes the leftmost syllable of a root the bearer of stress, stress being interpreted as long duration.]
sources.note: The paper is mainly about tone association and the OCP (tonal dissimilation/fusion) in Tikuna, with data from four Tikuna villages in Brazil, but its section on duration states the stress rule explicitly: long vowel duration is derived by a rule that makes the leftmost syllable of a root the bearer of stress, stress being interpreted (realised) as long duration (p. 21, citing Soares 1992a). The remainder of that section (pp. 21-23) treats binary right-to-left foot construction (moraic trochees per Hayes 1991) over the duration and pitch planes.
